extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, lawyers, tribunal staff, and policymakers working on Quebec social security/administrative appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive/legal guidance on the composition, organization, jurisdiction and procedure of the Commission des affaires sociales (SAC) for handling appeals in Quebec social-security and related administrative matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of decisions appealable to the SAC
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerates types of decisions that may be appealed to the SAC (e.g., decisions concerning mentally ill persons, recommendations made to health or social services establishments by regional councils following complaints, Quebec Health Insurance Board decisions concerning payment for professional services, contested elections and appointments to regional councils and boards of directors of establishments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists multiple specific categories to show the SAC's very varied jurisdiction; these categories determine whether a particular administrative decision may properly be brought before the SAC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility of SAC members to match varied jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the decisions appealable to the SAC are extremely varied and call for diverse forms of expertise, the composition and organization of the Commission are intended to ensure a high degree of versatility of SAC members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition/organization should provide the range of technical expertise needed for the multifarious powers exercised by the SAC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between members and assessors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act distinguishes between SAC 'members' (from whom the president and vice-president are chosen) and 'assessors', with different qualifications, roles and terms of office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members are jurists (lawyers) with certain full-time positions; assessors are technical specialists (e.g., physicians, psychiatrists, social workers) often part-time and assigned to specific divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership professional qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the SAC are to be lawyers; the president may be a judge; the president, vice-president and at least one other member are to devote themselves exclusively to SAC duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This professional composition is 'meant to guarantee the fairness of procedure and the effectiveness of the properly legal work of the SAC in hearing the cases appealed to it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessor professional qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessors' qualifications are specified (originally six physicians — including psychiatrists — and two social workers; later increases included more medical assessors), chosen to provide technical expertise needed for particular litigation areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors are selected to supply specialized expertise (medicine, psychiatry, social work) relevant to appeals (e.g., social aid, commitment orders, disability pensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Term limits for members and assessors
rubrics_metrics.description: No member of the SAC may hold office for a term exceeding ten years; no assessor may hold office for a term exceeding five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term limits are statutory; changes in staff numbers over time were effected but term ceilings remain as described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staffing levels and specialization into divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The SAC is structured into specialized divisions (originally four, later six): social aid and allowances; mental patients protection; health services and social services; pension plan; workmen's compensation; automobile insurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each division is called upon to rule on a specific category of appeals; the jurisdiction of each division is defined in the Act and cases may not be transferred from one division to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of members and assessors to divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Members are not assigned to a single division and typically participate in at least two divisions (most participate in all); assessors are assigned by the Cabinet to one or more specific divisions at appointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arrangement balances versatility (members) with targeted technical input (assessors). Assessors often continue private practice and participate part-time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quorum composition requirement (minimum jurist presence)
rubrics_metrics.description: One universal principle: the quorum must always include at least one Commission member (a jurist), as provided in the Act; the task of chairing is entrusted to a member appointed by the president.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quorum compositions are tailored to divisions' technical needs (examples: social aid division — one member + one assessor; mental patients protection — one member + two psychiatrist assessors; workmen's compensation & automobile insurance — two members + one medical assessor; pension plan — three members; health services division — variable compositions). In ties the president/vice-president has casting vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility to sit with additional members/assessors
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the quorum is the statutory minimum, a division may sit with additional members or assessors present, especially in difficult cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The quorum is the minimum required to give decisions legal force; expanding the panel is permissible and often used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of procedure across divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: SAC procedure is uniform in principle across its specialized divisions; although the Act authorizes a general meeting to lay down rules for each division, the SAC has adopted general internal regulations applying to all divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardization was an objective in creating the SAC; no substantive procedural distinctions are made between divisions in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental procedural principles: impartiality, right to be heard, written reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act lays down three fundamental principles: the duty of impartiality; the right of parties to be heard; the obligation to justify decisions in writing and transmit reasons to the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impartiality: members and assessors must be impartial and subject to recusation provisions in the Code of Civil Procedure. Right to be heard contemplates physical presence at hearing but may be waived; the obligation to give written reasons binds whether the appellant appeared or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration as common procedural formula
rubrics_metrics.description: A common procedural formula—the declaration—applies to all remedies under the Act (applications, requests, appeals). The declaration must indicate with sufficient clarity and precision the event giving rise to it and the reasons for contesting the decision; it must state whether the appellant intends to appear or be represented or to waive being heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A declaration form is available but not mandatory; the form is drafted in simple language and includes a list to help describe the contested decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to counsel and its administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties have the right to be represented by counsel; in the initial declaration the appellant must specify whether he wishes to be represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SAC has commented on the role of lawyers: while representation is increasing, the SAC asks lawyers to avoid confrontational, legalistic pleadings and pledges to facilitate hearings for unrepresented parties by actively conducting examinations and steering debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pension appeals treated as new applications (new trial approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: In appeals relating to pensions, the SAC considers cases as new applications for benefits, enabling evaluation of applicants' situations 'as of the day of the hearing' rather than only retrospectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'new trial' posture allows consideration of current circumstances and contributes to SAC's latitude in matters of form and substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formality liberalization and non-nullification for procedural defects
rubrics_metrics.description: The SAC's rules of procedure provide considerable latitude in matters of form; no proceedings are susceptible of being declared null and void because of a defect of form or procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects the objective of an accessible, flexible system 'devoid of formalism' to serve equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit for lodging appeals and extension for cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act prescribes a 90-day time limit from the date of the contested decision for lodging any appeal, with two statutory exceptions for certain action types; the SAC may entertain belated appeals if the appellant demonstrates circumstances that impeded earlier action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications for extension are decided on the merits and based on documents submitted either voluntarily or at the SAC's request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of appeal on execution of contested decision
rubrics_metrics.description: As a principle, initiation of appeal proceedings does not suspend execution of the contested decision; however, a member of the SAC may rule that the appeal will suspend execution in cases of undue hardship where the recipient depends on benefits for subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule has practical consequences where benefit cessation is involved; suspension for hardship has many precedents in social aid but had not been invoked for Quebec Pension Board decisions at the time discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad evidentiary powers (not bound by court rules of evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: In hearing appeals, the SAC may use powers of a commission of enquiry (including compelling witnesses to give testimony) and is free to admit any species of evidence it deems acceptable in the interest of justice; it is not bound by rules of evidence applicable to regular courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This confers wide latitude to admit relevant materials necessary for equitable decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to produce minutes of hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Although SAC decisions are final and without further appeal, the SAC is obliged to produce minutes of its hearings detailing the names of witnesses and the nature of documents submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These minutes support transparency and are part of the SAC's publication/record obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to revise own decisions 'for cause'
rubrics_metrics.description: The SAC has the power of revising its own decisions 'for cause'; the Act provides that the quorum for revision is the same as for the decision to be revised but does not specify whether the revising quorum must be the same persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If revision is preceded by reopening a hearing, the same persons would likely participate; SAC organization facilitates use of revision procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation/practice to publish decisions (digests)
rubrics_metrics.description: The SAC is obliged by its constitutive Act to publish its decisions; in practice this has been construed as producing a digest of the most important rulings rather than publishing all decisions in extenso.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission selects decisions to be published; each digest volume includes tables of acts/regulations cited, caselaw cited, and an analytical index by subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate scope: substantive review and power to substitute judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The SAC perceives itself as an appellate administrative tribunal exercising broad powers of substantive review — able to substitute its own judgment for that of the administrative authority whose decision is contested (citing section 23 of its Act) — rather than merely a supervisory body limited to legality-review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SAC has rejected interpretations that would limit it to reviewing irregular exercise of discretion; it treats its role as deciding 'the decision that should have been rendered in the first place.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral obligations on specialized legal issues (contributions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an appeal against a Reconsideration Committee of the QPB raises a question involving the payment of contributions, the SAC is obliged to refer the matter to the Pension Appeal Board (PAB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This referral mechanism preserves the correct allocation of specialized jurisdiction where statutory responsibility lies elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAC's role in recommending statutory/regulatory/practice changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitutive statute authorizes the SAC to make recommendations in its annual report to the Minister (and through him to the National Assembly) concerning statutes, regulations, directives and administrative practices governing its jurisdiction; the SAC has used reports to propose amendments, point out poor coordination, and suggest practical improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This collegial reflection draws on a comprehensive overview of social security functioning and may influence legislative/administrative reform over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and publication discretion over caselaw
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission assumes responsibility for selecting which decisions to publish in its digests and thereby exercises editorial judgment over the precedential materials it circulates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Quebec does not subscribe to stare decisis, publication is a tool to build systematic jurisprudence but does not bind the SAC to PAB precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority-setting and workload allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The SAC prioritized cases (initially social aid and mental patients protection) and allocated member time (e.g., pension plan division sittings one out of every two weeks) to reduce backlog; workload patterns influence which branches will produce more appeals and receive priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resource and scheduling decisions affect efficiency and the speed of disposition; backlog and transition effects are acknowledged.
